labels.og_answer: A big adult Triceratops was about 7 to 8 m (23 to 26 ft) long, with a skull about 2 m

top.answer: Big adult Triceratops were about 7 to 8 m (23 to 26 ft) long, and the largest reached about 9 m (30 ft). No Triceratops was ever weighed: two computer models of the famous Washington skeleton give about 6.5 to 8.5 tonnes. Our Triceratops is built after that skeleton, a mount of bones from about ten animals. It is 6.9 m (23 ft) long, about four people end to end, and stands about 2.5 m (8 ft) high over the hips.
top.answer_more: A big adult Triceratops skull is about 2 m (6.5 ft) long, beak to the back of the frill: longer than a person is tall. It is one of the largest heads of any land animal.

guess.q: What did the first scientist to study its horns think they came from?
guess.a: A giant bison: in 1887 the American scientist Othniel Marsh named the two horn cores Bison alticornis. After more finds he named Triceratops in 1889.

paras: A big adult's skull was about 2 m (6.5 ft) long, by a study of ten skulls from baby to adult. On the scan of the rebuilt Washington skull, we measure 2.12 m (7 ft) in bone.

Two long horns stand over the eyes and a short, low one on the nose. The long nose horn of many pictures belongs to the later species, Triceratops prorsus, and ours is the older Triceratops horridus. The bone in a museum is only the horn's core: in life a sheath of horn covered it, so the horns were longer, by how much nobody knows. They changed with age too: a young Triceratops's brow horns curved backward, an adult's forward.

The frill is a wide shield of solid bone behind the head, with no holes in it, under skin. What horns and frill were for, nobody has proved. The best evidence is healed wounds on frills, best explained by the horns of other Triceratops, so they most likely fought each other. Showing off and telling each other apart are likely uses too, and defence against predators is possible.

In one count of the large dinosaurs of Montana's Hell Creek Formation, where both lived at the same time, Triceratops was the most common of all. T. rex did bite Triceratops: a Triceratops hip bone found in 1991 carries 58 definite tooth marks that only a T. rex could have made, says a university's report of 1996. One brow horn, bitten off, healed afterwards, so at least one Triceratops survived a T. rex bite.

Whether T. rex mostly hunted them or mostly ate the dead, the bones do not say, and no find shows a fight between the two. The famous “Dueling Dinosaurs” from Montana, a Triceratops and a tyrannosaur found together, do not prove one either. Since 2025 their tyrannosaur is counted as Nanotyrannus, a smaller kind, not T. rex, and that is still argued.
Our two at one scale, for size only: our T. rex is about 1.6 times as long as our Triceratops.

scale.what: Our Triceratops and our T. rex to one scale, both facing the same way, with the person. Our T. rex, after SUE, is about 11 m (36 ft) long, about 1.6 times our Triceratops. Side by side for size only, never as a fight.

blocks.nav: Torosaurus: a very old Triceratops, or its own animal?
blocks.h: Torosaurus: a very old Triceratops, or its own animal?
paras: Torosaurus was a horned dinosaur from the same time and the same rocks, with a longer frill that had two big holes in it. In 2010 two scientists proposed that it was no separate animal, only a Triceratops grown very old, whose frill stretched and opened holes late in life. Later studies found young Torosaurus and old Triceratops, and measured skull shapes that grow apart, not together. A Torosaurus that was still young cannot have been an old Triceratops. Most scientists therefore now see Torosaurus as a separate animal, though the question is still argued and neither side counts as proven.

The skeleton in the Smithsonian's natural history museum in Washington is called Hatcher, after the fossil hunter John Bell Hatcher, and its bones came from Wyoming. It went on show in 1905, low and sprawling like a crocodile, and for over twenty years no other Triceratops was on show anywhere. No complete skeleton was known, so the museum pieced it together from about ten animals. Its skull was too small, its front legs of different lengths, and its hind feet, which came from another dinosaur, had the wrong count of toes.

In 1996 a piece of hip bone fell off: minerals growing inside the bones were breaking them up, and in 1998 the skeleton came down. Then, for the first time, a whole dinosaur skeleton was scanned in 3D, the skull enlarged by about 15 percent on the computer and the right side mirrored to make the left. After that the mount stood upright, and since 2019 Hatcher has lain in the fossil hall while a T. rex feeds on it: a museum's scene, not a find. Our Triceratops is built after that scan.

scale.what: Our Triceratops as a skeleton, with the person, after the Washington mount of about ten animals and the museum's scan of it. The pale shape behind it is our animal's outline. No bone-by-bone map is published: the skull is from one animal, most of the body from another, so no bone is coloured by its find. The horns are bone cores only: in life a cover of horn made them longer.
scale.alt: The skeleton of the Triceratops from the side, the big skull with its frill and horn cores, the ribs and four legs, beside the grey person, with the pale outline of its body behind the bones.

blocks.nav: What a real Triceratops looked like
blocks.h: What a real Triceratops looked like

paras: Scales up to 9 cm wide on the trunk, the largest ordinary scales known on any dinosaur, with a slightly bigger bumped scale every 15 to 20 cm. That comes from a clay cast of the skin's surface on another big Triceratops. Feathers or quills are unlikely.
A horny beak snipped plants, and rows of teeth at the back of the jaws cut them like shears.

The front legs stood upright under the body, elbows a little out, never sprawled like a lizard's, and two methods agree on that. Three of the five fingers and all four toes had hooves. No colour is known, so ours is a choice.

Triceratops lived in western North America in the Late Cretaceous, between about 68 and 66 million years ago. Two species followed each other: the older T. horridus, ours, slowly changed into the later T. prorsus. Its last fossils reach the close of the Cretaceous, about 66 million years ago, when an impact in the Yucatán is thought to have set off the collapse.

blocks.intro: For each number: where it came from, and what it means.

rows.text: A range many sites give, from popular dinosaur guides rather than measured skeletons. Named skeletons whose length is given run about 6.7 to 8 m (22 to 26 ft), so not even the largest of them reaches 9 m.
A round top figure for the largest, from a museum's dinosaur directory with no method and no skeleton named. A big adult was about 7 to 8 m, and ours is 6.9 m.

Printed beside the 9 m, again with no method. Many sites give 6 to 10 tonnes, a range from popular dinosaur guides, and some German ones a higher top figure from a study of 1985, which we have not read. The newest models of the Washington skeleton give about 6.5 to 8.5 tonnes.
A museum's card of the biggest dinosaurs, with no method, and above every other figure here.

rows.term: The largest head of any land animal
rows.text: One big museum says “one of the largest”, not “the largest”. Big adult skulls are about 2 m long.

The largest Triceratops skull known, estimated as it would be if complete, by a study of 2010. Most big adults' skulls are about 2 m long, and the rebuilt Washington skull that ours follows measures 2.12 m in bone on its scan.
It belongs to T. prorsus, the later species. T. horridus, the older one and ours, had a short, low horn on a long snout.
An idea of 2010. Later studies found young Torosaurus, and most keep the two apart.

blocks.intro: For each picture: where it came from, and what we know now.

rows.term: Small spikes all round the edge of the frill
rows.text: That fits a young Triceratops, whose frill had a scalloped edge ringed with 17 to 19 small bony points. In old adults the points had merged into the edge, which by then was wavy or smooth: the ten skulls from baby to adult show it.

rows.term: Quills or bristles along the back
rows.text: They were borrowed from Psittacosaurus, a small relative from much older rocks with bristles on its tail. Going by the shape of a big Triceratops's scales, one study finds such bristles unlikely.

Hooves, not claws, and the palms turned partly inward, going by one hand found with its bones in place. In horned dinosaurs found with whole feet the long foot bones lie close together, so most likely Triceratops had a compact foot, not the splayed one of many reconstructions.

rows.term: A bright frill with a red patch
rows.text: Most pictures show it so, but no pigment has ever been found in a Triceratops. The only horned dinosaur whose colours are known is the small Psittacosaurus, dark above and light below.

items.a: No height has been published, but on photographs of the Washington skeleton we read about 2.3 to 2.5 m (7.5 to 8 ft) at the top of the back over the hips. Ours, built after that skeleton, is 2.5 m (8 ft) there, about one and a half people high, and the top of its frill is about 2.4 m (7.8 ft) up.

items.q: Was Triceratops bigger than T. rex?
items.a: No. A big adult Triceratops was about 7 to 8 m (23 to 26 ft) long, a large T. rex about 12 m (39 ft) and far higher at the hips. In weight they were closer: about 6.5 to 8.5 tonnes for the Washington Triceratops, about 8 to 9 for a large T. rex. Only the skull was longer: about 2 m against SUE's 1.4 m.

items.q: What does the name Triceratops mean?
items.a: Three-horned face, from Greek. Marsh gave the name in 1889, and ours is Triceratops horridus, the older of its two species.

paras: Museum of Ages is a digital museum, made by a nonprofit. Free entry, no account. In the animal wing this animal will stand among the others, from the giants of long ago to the last of their kind. The Leonardo da Vinci wing shows what a finished wing looks like.

items.alt: Our T. rex from the side on two legs, about 11 m (36 ft) long in this pose, mouth closed and head raised, beside a grey person 1.70 m tall who stands far below its hips.
items.line: A large adult T. rex was about 12 m long, about 4 m at the hips and roughly 8 to 9 tonnes. Our T. rex is built to SUE's measurements and stands beside a person to one scale, with a list of what was found of SUE.

items.alt: Our seven dinosaurs in a row from the side, to one scale. The longest, our Argentinosaurus, is about 30.6 m (100 ft) long. Two long necks tower over the rest, and a grey person 1.70 m tall looks tiny beside them.
items.line: Seven of ours beside a person, to one scale: the heaviest most likely a titanosaur from Patagonia, the tallest probably Sauroposeidon, and why the longest is still open.

items.alt: Our Brachiosaurus from the side, built at the Chicago skeleton's size, 24.0 m (79 ft) along the backbone, its long neck raised in a gentle curve to a head top 11.5 m (38 ft) up, the neck angle our choice. The front legs are longer than the hind legs, the tail is off the ground, and a grey person 1.70 m tall could walk under its belly.
items.line: Brachiosaurus, a long-necked plant eater of the Late Jurassic, was about 22 to 25 m long and roughly 30 to 45 tonnes, both figures rebuilt from one partial skeleton. Our Brachiosaurus stands beside a person, its head about seven people up in the pose we chose.

items.alt: Our Ankylosaurus from the side, 6.4 m (21 ft) from beak to club, its back 1.7 m (5.6 ft) high over the hips: a low, wide body under rows of bony plates, a broad head carried low, four short legs and a straight tail ending in a flat club. Beside it a grey person 1.70 m tall, as tall as the top of its back.
items.line: Ankylosaurus, a club-tailed plant eater whose bones lie in the same rocks as those of Triceratops, was about 6 to 8 m long. Our Ankylosaurus stands beside a person to one scale, with its club, its armour and what was found.

items.alt: Our Stegosaurus from the side, 5.6 m (18 ft) from beak to tail tip, its back 1.9 m (6.4 ft) high over the hips: a small low head, two rows of tall plates along the arched back, two of its four tail spikes, the front legs shorter than the hind legs. Beside it a grey person 1.70 m tall whose head stays below the top of its back.
items.line: The largest Stegosaurus were about 9 m long, and Sophie, the skeleton in London, is about 5.6 m. Our Stegosaurus stands beside our Triceratops to one scale, with the roughly 80 million years that kept the two apart.
